title: Galilee Gt
subject: Torts
stem:
BARMATRIX Q#: 15263_galilee_gt

Lydia, who was 20 years old, purchased a new, high-powered sports car called the Galilee GT, which was marketed with an intended and recognized appeal to youthful drivers, including ads showing college students driving to Christian music festivals. The car was designed with the capability to attain speeds in excess of 100 miles per hour. It was equipped with tires designed and tested only for a maximum safe speed of 85 miles per hour.

The owner’s manual that came with the car stated that “continuous driving over 90 miles per hour requires high-speed-capability tires,” but the manual did not describe the speed capability of the tires sold with the car.

Lydia took her new car out for a drive on a straight, smooth country road where the posted speed limit was 55 miles per hour. Intending to test the car’s power, she drove for a considerable distance at over 100 miles per hour. While she was doing so, the tread separated from the left rear tire, causing the car to leave the road and hit a tree. Lydia sustained severe injuries.

Lydia has brought a strict product liability action in tort against the manufacturer of the car. Assume that pure comparative fault principles apply.

Will Lydia prevail?
call: Will Lydia prevail in her strict product liability action against the manufacturer?

choices.A: No, because Lydia's driving at an excessive speed constituted a misuse of the car.
choices.B: No, because the car was not defective.
choices.C: Yes, because the statement in the manual concerning the tires did not adequately warn of the danger of high-speed driving on the tires mounted on the car.
choices.D: No, because Lydia's driving at a speed in excess of the posted speed limit was negligence per se that was not excusable.

rightExplanation:
C is correct.

Gold Key: Foreseeable misuse / warning defect. A manufacturer cannot escape a warning-defect strict-liability claim merely by calling the plaintiff’s use “misuse” when the use was foreseeable from the product’s design, marketing, and manual. If the product’s danger could have been reduced by a clearer warning, the warning failure can make the product defective.

Silver Key: When the answer set fights between “misuse” and “inadequate warning,” go back to the stem and ask whether the manufacturer invited or forecasted the dangerous use. Here, the car could exceed 100 mph, was marketed to youthful drivers, and the manual itself mentioned high-speed tires without telling Lydia that the installed tires were not high-speed-capability tires.

Lydia’s speeding may affect damages under pure comparative fault, but it does not defeat liability at the “will she prevail?” stage.

wrongExplanations.A: This answer says “misuse,” but it does not answer the decisive question: whether the use was unforeseeable. Gold Key: foreseeable misuse is not a complete bar to a warning-defect strict-liability claim. Silver Key: the stem’s design/marketing/manual facts point away from a complete “misuse” bar.
wrongExplanations.B: This answer treats “defective” as only a physical design or manufacturing problem. That misses the warning-defect lane. A product can be defective because the warning or instructions are inadequate, even if the object itself performs as designed.
wrongExplanations.D: This answer imports negligence-per-se language and makes it a complete bar. But the call asks whether Lydia will prevail in strict product liability, and the stem gives pure comparative fault. At most, her fault can reduce damages; it does not automatically defeat the claim.

c3.label: CUT B
c3.text: B talks only like “no physical defect.” It misses the warning-defect lane. Cut as wrong element once the warning-defect anchor is active.

c3.label: CUT D
c3.text: D gives a negligence-per-se reason and treats it as a total bar. But the stem gives pure comparative fault. Cut as bait doctrine / wrong remedy.

c3.label: CLASH A vs. C
c3.text:
A says “misuse defeats.” C says “warning defect wins.”
Axis: foreseeable high-speed use vs. unforeseeable misuse.
Fact: the car was built and marketed for high-speed appeal, and the manual itself warned vaguely about high-speed tires.
Resolver: use was foreseeable. C wins.

c3.label: CALL
c3.text: No unresolved fork. Anchor-assisted residual is C.

studentScript: The call is strict product liability, not whether Lydia was negligent. A says misuse, but the stem makes speed foreseeable. B ignores warning defect. D turns comparative fault into a bar. C uses the warning facts. Pick C.

A.signal: The answer names user fault but skips the resolving fact: the manufacturer built, marketed, and warned around high-speed use.
A.lawyer: Misuse defeats only when it removes foreseeability or causation; foreseeable use/misuse does not bar warning-defect liability.

B.signal: The answer treats defect as only the car's hardware, but the call and stem include a manual warning problem.
B.lawyer: A product can be defective through inadequate instructions or warnings.

C.signal: This answer uses the stem's exact risk: high-speed tires, installed tire capacity, and incomplete warning.
C.lawyer: This is the proper strict products warning-defect theory.

D.signal: The answer answers plaintiff fault as a complete defeat, but the stem says pure comparative fault.
D.lawyer: Plaintiff negligence may reduce damages; it does not automatically defeat strict product liability under pure comparative fault.

goldKeys.statement: In a strict products warning-defect case, foreseeable high-risk use or foreseeable misuse is not a complete bar; pure comparative fault may reduce damages, but inadequate warnings can still make the product defective.
goldKeys.trigger: Product marketed or designed for the same dangerous use the plaintiff attempted
goldKeys.authority: Restatement (Third) of Torts: Products Liability § 2(c); Daly v. General Motors; comparative-fault products-liability authorities

silverKeys.statement: When one answer says misuse and another says inadequate warning, stop debating blame and find whether the seller invited or forecasted that use in the stem.
silverKeys.trigger: Answer set contains both misuse and warning-defect explanations

remediation.title: Do not turn foreseeable misuse into a total bar.
remediation.signal: Product built/marketed for the dangerous use + incomplete warning
remediation.studentMove: Name the clash: misuse bar vs warning defect. Then read for manufacturer-invited use.
remediation.tinyRule: Foreseeable use keeps the warning-defect lane alive.
